title: From Physical Infrastructure to Population-Scale Tech Rails: India Offers a Transformative Growth Story to the World, says Union Minister of State for Communications, Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani
subtitle:
Digital Public Infrastructure is a Necessity, not a Luxury, for Sustainable Development Across the Global South: Union MoS, Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani
Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani delivers keynote address on sustainable and resilient digital and ICT ecosystems at BRICS ICT Track in Pune
body_text:
Union Minister of State for Communications, Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani, delivered a keynote address today at the BRICS ICT Track Thematic Panel Discussion on "Sustainable and Resilient Digital and ICT Ecosystems: Digital Public Infrastructure for Impact – Global South Insights on Powering Public Services and Economic Growth" held in Pune.
Addressing an international delegation comprising ministers, policymakers, academicians, and industry leaders from BRICS nations, the Union Minister of State outlined India’s strategic vision for open, inclusive, and resilient digital architectures designed to empower citizens and accelerate economic progress.
Highlighting India’s transformative journey, Dr Pemmasani stated that while the conventional narrative of infrastructure historically revolved around physical assets like roads, ports, and power grids, India has demonstrated a modern paradigm built on population-scale digital rails encompassing identity, banking, payments, verifiable documents, and consented data.
He noted that the true innovation lies in establishing an open, interoperable foundational public layer upon which banks, fintech enterprises, and government departments can build diverse consumer services under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi.
Elaborating on the core pillars of India’s Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), the Union MoS detailed how the foundational identity layer enables low-cost remote verification across billions of authentications, SIM issuances, and banking access. In the payments sphere, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has democratized finance, linking 720 banks, processing 85% of India’s digital transactions, and contributing to nearly 49% of global real-time payment volumes while expanding to nine partner nations.
He also emphasized the role of the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) portal, which integrates 318 schemes across 56 ministries to eliminate intermediaries, alongside DigiLocker’s ecosystem of over 700 million users and 9 billion issued verifiable credentials. Newer initiatives such as the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC), Government e-Marketplace (GeM), and Account Aggregator framework are further democratizing market access and individual data sovereignty.
Underpinning these software innovations is India’s robust telecommunications expansion. The Union Minister of State highlighted that 4G mobile coverage now spans nearly 99% of villages, backed by a $4 billion saturation drive, while the nation has accomplished one of the fastest global 5G rollouts with over 500,000 base stations deployed. Concurrently, a $17 billion BharatNet mission is laying high-speed optical fibre across every major village. On environmental sustainability, Dr Pemmasani shared that India has already achieved 12.4% green energy usage across mobile towers against a national mandate of powering 30% of telecom infrastructure through renewable sources by 2030.
Concluding his address, Dr Pemmasani stressed that DPI is not a luxury reserved for advanced economies, but an imperative for sustainable development across the Global South. He called for a stronger BRICS digital partnership anchored in sharing modular, open-source technology frameworks to eliminate prohibitive licensing costs, alongside joint capacity-building initiatives to ensure fair representation in international ICT standard-setting bodies.
The thematic panel session witnessed the participation of distinguished international dignitaries and BRICS representatives, including Mr Frederico de Siqueira Filho, Minister of Communications of the Federative Republic of Brazil, and Mr Mondli Gungubele, Deputy Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies of the Republic of South Africa, among other ministerial delegates and global technology leaders.

enrichment.summary: Union Minister of State for Communications Dr Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani delivered a keynote at the BRICS ICT Track's thematic panel in Pune on 'Sustainable and Resilient Digital and ICT Ecosystems,' presenting India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) model to BRICS delegates including ministers from Brazil and South Africa. He cited key statistics: UPI links 720 banks and handles 85% of India's digital transactions and ~49% of global real-time payments; DBT integrates 318 schemes across 56 ministries; DigiLocker has over 700 million users and 9 billion credentials issued; 4G covers 99% of villages; over 500,000 5G base stations are deployed; BharatNet is a $17 billion optical fibre mission; and mobile towers use 12.4% green energy against a 30%-by-2030 target. He called for BRICS cooperation on open-source DPI frameworks and fair representation in global ICT standard-setting.
enrichment.context: India's Digital Public Infrastructure model—anchored in Aadhaar (identity), UPI (payments), and DigiLocker/DEPA (data)—has become a globally cited example of 'population-scale' digital rails and is increasingly promoted internationally, including through G20 and now BRICS forums, as a template for the Global South. This reflects India's diplomatic push to position DPI as a public good and export India's stack to developing nations, building on prior G20 presidency commitments on DPI. The mention of specific figures (UPI's 85% share of digital transactions, DBT's 318 schemes, DigiLocker's 700 million users) is useful for aspirants tracking DPI's scale, while the telecom figures (99% village 4G coverage, BharatNet's $17 billion outlay, and the 30% renewable energy target for telecom infrastructure by 2030) tie into India's Digital India and telecom sustainability goals. This event itself is a speech at an international forum rather than a new policy announcement, but the aggregated statistics on DPI and telecom infrastructure make it a useful factual reference point for current affairs preparation on India's digital governance architecture and its global outreach through BRICS.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following statements about India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), as highlighted at the BRICS ICT Track in Pune, is correct?
options: UPI accounts for nearly 49% of global real-time payment volumes
DigiLocker has issued over 700 million verifiable credentials
BharatNet is a $4 billion mission for optical fibre connectivity
DBT portal integrates schemes across 30 ministries only
prelims_questions.explanation: As per the release, UPI contributes nearly 49% of global real-time payment volumes; DigiLocker has over 700 million users (not credentials) and 9 billion credentials issued; BharatNet is a $17 billion mission; DBT integrates 318 schemes across 56 ministries, not 30.

prelims_questions.question: India's national target for powering telecom infrastructure through renewable energy sources by 2030, as mentioned in the release, is:
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states India has a national mandate to power 30% of telecom infrastructure through renewable sources by 2030, against a current achievement of 12.4%.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) model in promoting financial inclusion and service delivery. How can India leverage platforms like BRICS to export this model to the Global South?
Examine the role of foundational digital identity, payment, and data-sharing systems in transforming governance and public service delivery in India, with suitable examples.

study_notes.reason: The release is essentially a data-dump speech on India's DPI and telecom statistics with limited independent analytical content beyond generic calls for cooperation; its value lies in the concrete facts and figures an aspirant could be tested on.

prelims.point: Unified Payments Interface (UPI) links 720 banks, processes 85% of India's digital transactions, and accounts for ~49% of global real-time payment volume
prelims.why_important: UPI's scale and global real-time payments share is a frequently cited statistic for India's DPI and digital economy questions.

prelims.point: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) portal integrates 318 schemes across 56 ministries
prelims.why_important: DBT architecture and its scale is relevant to questions on welfare delivery and reducing leakages.

prelims.point: DigiLocker has over 700 million users and has issued over 9 billion verifiable credentials
prelims.why_important: DigiLocker is a core DPI pillar for data/document verification, useful for questions on India's digital identity ecosystem.

prelims.point: 4G mobile coverage spans nearly 99% of villages, achieved via a $4 billion saturation drive
prelims.why_important: Reflects telecom penetration milestones often quoted in Digital India progress questions.

prelims.point: BharatNet is a $17 billion mission for high-speed optical fibre connectivity to villages
prelims.why_important: BharatNet is a flagship rural broadband scheme frequently referenced in governance and infrastructure questions.

prelims.point: India has deployed over 500,000 5G base stations, marking one of the fastest global 5G rollouts
prelims.why_important: 5G rollout scale is a testable fact on India's telecom infrastructure achievements.

prelims.point: Telecom towers currently use 12.4% green energy against a national target of 30% renewable-powered telecom infrastructure by 2030
prelims.why_important: Distinguishes current status from target figure, a classic UPSC pattern of testing progress versus goal.

prelims.point: India's DPI model is built on three pillars: identity (Aadhaar), payments (UPI), and data/documents (DigiLocker/Account Aggregator)
prelims.why_important: This foundational DPI framework is essential background for any question on India's digital public infrastructure architecture.

mains.point: India is positioning its DPI model as an exportable public good for the Global South through platforms like BRICS, following earlier G20 advocacy
mains.theme: Digital diplomacy and Global South leadership
mains.analytical_use: Useful for answers on India's soft power projection and leadership role in multilateral digital governance forums.

mains.point: Call for BRICS cooperation on open-source, modular DPI frameworks to eliminate licensing costs for developing nations
mains.analytical_use: Supports answers on technology transfer, affordability of digital infrastructure, and BRICS as an alternative cooperation framework.

mains.point: Push for fairer representation of developing countries in international ICT standard-setting bodies
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on reforming global institutions and addressing asymmetries in technology rule-making.

low_priority.point: Names and designations of foreign dignitaries attending the panel (Brazil, South Africa ministers)
low_priority.reason: Ceremonial participant details with no factual or analytical exam value.

low_priority.point: General rhetorical framing about India's leadership under the Prime Minister
low_priority.reason: Political messaging without new policy substance.

related_articles.title: Mobile and Internet Connectivity in Tribal Areas
related_articles.relationship: Both releases come from the telecom sector and reference India's 4G/5G rural coverage push; the earlier release detailed Digital Bharat Nidhi-funded 4G/5G tower rollout in tribal areas, aligning with the new release's citation of 99% village-level 4G coverage as part of India's digital infrastructure story.
